There were a variety of names for the Guadalquivir in Classical and pre-Classical times. [image alt: Eine lebhafte und etwas chaotische Szene auf einem Fluss, die auf der Ibar-Regatta in Serbien aufgenommen wurde.
​Mehrere gelbe und schwarze Schlauchboote treiben dicht aneinandergedrängt auf dem grünen Wasser. Die Boote sind voll besetzt mit Menschen in Sommerkleidung, die feiern und sich zwischen den Booten die Hände reichen.
​Das Besondere an der Szene ist eine komplette Blaskapelle (Trubači), die mit ihren großen Blechblasinstrumenten (Tuben, Trompeten) und einer Basstrommel mitten auf den wackeligen Schlauchbooten sitzt und musiziert. Auf der Trommel ist in kyrillischer Schrift der Name des Orchesters ("Orkestar Dragana...") zu erkennen. Im Hintergrund schwenkt ein Mann auf einem anderen Boot eine serbische Fahne an einem langen Stock.]

posts.text: The Ottawa. 🥰
posts.fullText:
The Ottawa. 🥰
[image alt: Dear dark-brown waters full of all the stain
Of sombre spruce-woods and the forest fens,
Laden with sound from far-off northern glens
Where winds and craggy cataracts complain,
Voices of streams and mountain pines astrain,
The pines that brood above the roaring foam
Of La Montagne or Les Erables; thine home
Is distant yet, a shelter far to gain.
Aye still to eastward, past the shadowy lake
And the long slopes of Rigaud toward the sun,
The mightier stream, thy comrade, waits for thee,
The beryl waters that espouse and take
Thine in their deep embrace, and bear thee on
In that great bridal journey to the sea.]

posts.text: No, there isn't. All the water from Lake George flows North into Lake Champlain and eventually into the St. Lawrence River. The Hudson River flows South, with a little detour East between Corinth and Hudson Falls (just North of Fort Edward). The two watersheds don't connect at all.

posts.text: It's online, actually. One of several tools I use in the course of my work as a survey and civil engineering drafter. You need the Federal township survey because the whole country west of the Ohio River and not including acknowledged Native land and already settled by white folks land was divided.
posts.fullText: It's online, actually. One of several tools I use in the course of my work as a survey and civil engineering drafter. You need the Federal township survey because the whole country west of the Ohio River and not including acknowledged Native land and already settled by white folks land was divided.

posts.text: It was divided into mile-across squares, called sections, each within 6*6 mile squares called (survey) townships. Not to be confused with political townships whose territory isn't alway exactly a survey township because, well, politics.
posts.fullText: It was divided into mile-across squares, called sections, each within 6*6 mile squares called (survey) townships. Not to be confused with political townships whose territory isn't alway exactly a survey township because, well, politics.

posts.text: The problem with putting a grid of mile squares across thousands of miles of land is that the earth is spherical. (And also surveyors make mistakes and/or are drunk, and are measuring with compasses and literal chains). The corners don't always meet. The township maps tell you what the offsets are.
posts.fullText: The problem with putting a grid of mile squares across thousands of miles of land is that the earth is spherical. (And also surveyors make mistakes and/or are drunk, and are measuring with compasses and literal chains). The corners don't always meet. The township maps tell you what the offsets are.

posts.text: So if I'm drawing up a plat of a piece of land on a township corner, and the surveyor says "found a disk" (or nail or whatever) that's supposed to be at the corner, I get to look it up to see WHICH corner it is, because sometimes the SW corner of Township A is 20 feet from the SE corner of Twp B.

Technically I lived in Vancouver proper, but I liked this photo and have spent a lot of time in New West and Surrey.]
[image alt: The Chattahoochee river, just outside of Atlanta, Georgia]
[image alt: The Charles river flowing through Cambridge and Boston, MA. The Harvard campus is in the foreground and Downtown Boston and Back Bay loom in the background. 

I realized, I knew the indigenous names for the Fraser and the North Saskatchewan, but not the Charles so I decided to search it up. Turns out, the Massachusett people called it "Quinobequin". The more you know!]

[image alt: History
The word "Connecticut" is a corruption of the Mohegan word quinetucket and Nipmuc word kwinitekw, which mean "beside the long, tidal river".[8][9] The word came into English usage during the early 1600s to name the river, which was also called simply "The Great River". It was also known by New Netherlanders as Versche Rivier, or the fresh river.[10]

Early spellings of the name by European explorers included "Cannitticutt" in French[11] or in English.[12]]

posts.text:
Me, I come from a dead river, drunk dry to feed corn to cows and cars.

My childhood was spent watching it die.

Freshwater clams, crayfish, darters, madtoms, shinners, sunfish, multicolored leaches, mayfly larva, water beetles, waterbugs, water striders.

All turned dust and sand.
